rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafaji rejects attaching the exception to nonperformance: Sunnis and Muʿtazilites alike cannot make that a coherent prohibition, since God can prevent an intended act through death or another impediment.
rows.anchor: وقال الخفاجي : إذا كان الاستثناء متعلقا بأني فاعل والمشيئة متعلقة بالعدم

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: He also rejects reading the verse as forbidding a Muʿtazilite to claim independent authorship whenever God's will does not accompany the act.
rows.anchor: فيضيفها لنفسه قائلا إن لم تقترن مشيئة الله تعالى بالفعل فأنا فاعله استقلالا

rows.speaker: الاعتراض على المعتزلة
rows.claim: A familiar objection says that if God wills only obedience, a debtor who vows to pay tomorrow if God wills must be perjured when he fails to pay, making the exception ineffective; it is like a condition whose condition occurs.
rows.anchor: لو كان كذلك لوجب فيما إذا قال : الذي عليه دين لغيره قد طالبه به

rows.speaker: المرتضى
rows.claim: Al-Murtaḍā distinguishes exceptions that suspend the legal force of oaths, contracts, and reports; this use may be retrospective but is unsuitable for sins because it displays reliance on God.
rows.anchor: بأن للاستثناء الداخل في الكلام وجوها مختلفة فقد يدخل في الأيمان والطلاق والعتاق

rows.speaker: المرتضى
rows.claim: A second use in permitted matters asks God to enable the act and preserve the existing state; al-Murtaḍā considers this possible in the verse.
rows.anchor: وقد يدخل في الكلام ويراد به التسهيل والأقدار والتخلية والبقاء على ما هو عليه من الأحوال

rows.speaker: المرتضى
rows.claim: A third use merely expresses reliance on God without deciding whether the statement is true or false, and could also fit the verse.
rows.anchor: وقد يدخل لمجرد غرض الانقطاع إلى الله تعالى ويكون على هذا غير معتمد به

rows.speaker: المرتضى
rows.claim: A fourth use seeks divine grace and facilitation, which applies only to obedience and cannot explain the verse's broader scope; if the debtor intended another sense, he need not be perjured.
rows.anchor: وقد يدخل ويراد به اللطف والتسهيل وهذا يختص بالطاعات ولا يصح أن تحمل الآية عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the objection and this answer are unpersuasive, and the Muʿtazilite position can be refuted without them.
rows.anchor: والانصاف أن الاعتراض ليس بشيء والرد عليهم غني عن مثل ذلك

rows.speaker: السيرافي
rows.claim: Using exception for qualification by saying if God wills, and for qualification by a condition generally, is established in Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: إطلاق الاستثناء على التقييد بإن شاء الله تعالى بل على التقييد بالشرط مطلقا ثابت في اللغة والاستعمال

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib defines exception as removing what a preceding general statement entails, as in the verse about what may be eaten, or what a particular utterance entails, as in a conditional divorce.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب : الاستثناء دفع ما يوجبه عموم سابق كما في قوله تعالى : ( قل لا أجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophetic report says that whoever swears to something and says if God wills has made an exception; al-Ālūsī therefore rejects explanations that call the phrase an exception only because of its Quranic wording or resemblance.
rows.anchor: من حلف على شيء فقال : إن شاء الله تعالى فقد استثنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering the Lord means remembering His will, with an omitted genitive; the preceding command is to say if God wills, as the Prophet did when this verse came down.
rows.anchor: أي مشيئة ربك فالكلام على حذف مضاف وذكر مشيئته تعالى على ما يدل عليه ما قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forgetting means an inadvertent omission; the command applies upon remembering, not during forgetfulness, and requires recovery whether the interval is short or long.
rows.anchor: إذا فرط منك نسيان ذلك ثم تذكرته فإنه مادام ناسيا لا يؤمر بالذكر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās held that a person may add the exception even after a year; this is also reported from the Imams of the Prophet's family and as one narration from Aḥmad.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما أنه كان يرى الاستثناء ولو بعد سنة ويقرأ الآية

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr says a person who swore and forgot to except retains the right of exception for a month.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر عن ابن جبير في رجل حلف ونسي أن يستثني قال : له ثنياه إلى شهر

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ, reporting from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, allows the exception for as long as it takes to milk a camel.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي حاتم من طريق عمرو بن دينار عن عطاء أنه قال : من حلف على يمين فله الثنيا حلب ناقة

rows.speaker: طاوس
rows.claim: Ṭāwūs limits the exception to the time a person remains in the same sitting.
rows.anchor: وكان طاوس يقول ما دام في مجلسه

rows.speaker: إبراهيم
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm says the exception is available only while the person is still speaking.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي حاتم أيضا عن إبراهيم قال : يستثنى ما دام في كلامه

rows.speaker: عامة الفقهاء
rows.claim: Most jurists require the exception to be connected to the oath; allowing it after any delay would undermine the finality of acknowledgments, divorce, emancipation, and truthful or false statements.
rows.anchor: وعامة الفقهاء على اشتراط اتصال الاستثناء في عدم الحنث ولو صح جواز الفصل وعدم تأثيره في الأحكام

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: In a story, Abū Ḥanīfa answers al-Manṣūr's objection to his disagreement with Ibn ʿAbbās by warning that delayed exceptions would let people leave a pledge of allegiance and then break it; al-Manṣūr approves the answer.
rows.anchor: فقال له أبو حنيفة : هذا يرجع إليك إنك تأخذ البيعة بالأيمان أفترضى أن يخرجوا من عندك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A traveler from the Maghrib hears two Baghdad vegetable sellers debate delayed exceptions: one argues that Job would have been told to except if Ibn ʿAbbās were right, since the remedy in the verse about his oath came after a year.
rows.anchor: ومن غريب ما يحكى أن رجلا من علماء المغرب أحب أن يرى علماء بغداد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The traveler returns home impressed that even a street seller could challenge Ibn ʿAbbās, and infers how learned Baghdad's scholars must be.
rows.anchor: رأيت من يبيع على رأسه في الطرقات من أهلها بلغ مبلغا من العلم يعترض به على ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says such an objection is excessive even from a vegetable seller and cautions that God knows whether the anecdote is authentic.
rows.anchor: والانصاف أن هذا الاعتراض على علامة يستكثر ممن يبيع البقل والله تعالى أعلم بصحة النقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent verse and report may seem to support Ibn ʿAbbās, but the required recovery is only a renewed declaration of dependence on God, not a delayed change to legal effect; the passage does not address legal rulings.
rows.anchor: إن التدارك فيما يرجع إلى تفويض العبد يحصل بذكره بعد التنبه أما في التأثير في الحكم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says that one who forgot the exception should make it when remembering, but that this privilege belongs only to the Prophet; others may except only as part of an oath.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما أنه قال في الآية : إذا نسيت الاستثناء فاستثن إذا ذكرت

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An alternative says the later words attach to an implied recurring statement: whenever one forgets God, remember Him upon recollection, or say if God wills when announcing a future act; al-Ālūsī finds this far from the apparent sense.
rows.anchor: وقيل ليس في الآية والخبر أن الاستثناء المتدارك من القول السابق بل من مقدر مدلول به عليه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One interpretation makes remembering the Lord mean glorifying and seeking forgiveness after forgetting the exception, urging it by implying that its omission merits repentance.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون المعنى واذكر ربك بالتسبيح والاستغفار إذا نسيت الاستثناء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another reads the command as remembering God and His punishment after leaving an instruction, to prompt correction; forgetfulness here is figurative for leaving something.
rows.anchor: وقيل المعنى واذكر ربك وعقابه إذا تركت بعض ما أمرك به ليبعثك ذلك على التدارك

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A further reading says to remember God when forgetfulness comes so He may remind the person of what was forgotten; it treats forgetfulness as intransitive, but connects poorly to the context.
rows.anchor: أو اذكر ربك إذا عرض لك نسيان ليذكرك المنسي و ( نيست ) على هذا منزل منزلة اللازم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda takes the verse to command making up a missed prayer when one remembers it; al-Ālūsī says this seems to be his intended reading and has the same weak contextual connection.
rows.anchor: وحمل قتادة الآية على أداء الصلاة المنسية عند ذكرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Qatāda instead infers prayer's make-up from the command to remember a forgotten exception, the analogy is more plausible because prayer merits greater concern, though this is not the apparent report.
rows.anchor: وإن أراد أنها تدل على الأمر بقضاء الصلاة المنسية عند ذكرها لما أنها دلت على الأمر بذكر الاستثناء المنسي

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima interprets the verse as remembering God when angry, since anger can cause forgetfulness; al-Ālūsī regards its contextual problem as like the prior interpretations.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي شيبة والبيهقي في شعب الإيمان وغيرهما عن عكرمة أنه قال في الآية : أي اذكر ربك إذا غضبت

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj reads the prayer for guidance as asking God to grant a sign more evident than the account of the Companions of the Cave, proving the Prophet's mission and guiding people.
rows.anchor: أي يوفقني ( لأقرب من هذا ( أي لشيء أقرب وأظهر من نبأ أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God later gave the Prophet clearer signs, including accounts of distant prophets and future events through the Resurrection; the wording also gently reduces the cave story's apparent wonder, as did the opening question.
rows.anchor: وقد فعل ذلك عز وجل حيث آتاه من الآيات البينات ما هو أعظم من ذلك وأبين كقصص الأنبياء

rows.speaker: بعض الأفاضل
rows.claim: One syntactic proposal links the prayer for guidance back to the command to recall when the youths took refuge in the cave: tell that story and hope for a clearer sign.
rows.anchor: على العامل في قوله تعالى ( إذ أوى الفتية إلى الكهف ) كأنه قيل اذكر إذ أوى الفتية

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī links the guidance prayer to remembering God: ask God to remind the Prophet of a forgotten matter, and if not, to guide him to something nearer and more beneficial; al-Ālūsī finds this closer syntactically but distant in other respects.
rows.anchor: وقال الجبائي : هو متعلق بقوله تعالى ( واذكر ربك ) إلى آخره والمعنى عنده ادع ربك

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another proposal links it to the preceding commands and prohibitions: hope for guidance to what is more beneficial than their instruction; al-Ālūsī judges this strained.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنه متعلق بالمتعاطفات قبله و ( هذا ) إشارة إلى ما تضمنته من الخير أمرا ونهيا

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī says God may reveal answers to the questioners before the promised time and hasten guidance; al-Ālūsī says the meaning cannot be derived and would make the Quran like a riddle.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري : معنى الآية عسى أن يعرفني ربي جواب مسائلكم قبل الوقت الذي حددته لكم

rows.speaker: رجل من أهل الكوفة
rows.claim: An unnamed Kufan, transmitted through Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān and his father and attributed by Abū Ḥayyān to Muḥammad al-Kūfī, says repentance for forgetting the exception is to recite the guidance prayer; al-Ālūsī says it has no evidence.
rows.anchor: وأخرج البيهقي من طريق المعتمر بن سليمان قال : سمعت أبي يحدث عن رجل من أهل الكوفة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The statement that the youths stayed three hundred years and nine more is an independent sentence explaining the earlier summary that God kept them asleep for a number of years; Mujāhid is cited for this explanation, which several scholars choose.
rows.anchor: وهي جملة مستأنفة مبينة كما قال مجاهد لما أجمل في قوله تعالى ( فضربنا على آذانهم في الكهف سنين عددا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to say that God knows best confirms the period already given as the true duration of their sleep; delaying the clarification signals disagreement over duration and marks this hidden report as a prophetic miracle, echoing the earlier conclusion about their number.
rows.anchor: تقرير لكون المدة المضروب فيها على آذانهم هي هذه المدة كأنه قيل قل الله أعلم بما لبثوا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The nine years may reconcile the solar-year count of the People of Scripture with the lunar-year count of Arabs, and this explanation is attributed by some to ʿAlī; al-Ālūsī details astronomical objections to the claimed nine-year difference.
rows.anchor: فقيل هو الإشارة إلى أنها ثلثمائة بحساب أهل الكتاب واعتبار السنة الشمسية وثلثمائة وتسع بحساب العرب

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafājī says the two counts are explicit in context: three hundred by the People of the Book's reckoning, then nine extra by the questioners' reckoning; the difference is approximate because the remaining fraction is below half a year.
rows.anchor: وبحث فيه الخفاجي بأن وجه الدلالة فيه ظاهر لأن المعنى لبثوا ثلثمائة سنة

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭībī proposes that the sleepers nearly awoke after three hundred years but something kept them sleeping nine additional years; al-Ālūsī objects that the verse would then need to say their sleep increased.
rows.anchor: وقال الطيبي في توجيه العدول : إنه يمكن أن يقال : لعلهم لما استكملوا ثلثمائة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the nine-year sleep-extension proposal because it would require an unexpressed meaning, that their sleep itself grew stronger for nine years.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأن هذا يقتضي أن يكون المراد وازدادوا نوما أي قوى نومهم في تسع سنين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the People of the Book disagreed over the sleepers' duration as they did their number; the verse resolves the disagreement, and the nine-year phrase confirms the answer like the exception in the account of Noah's thousand years.
rows.anchor: وقال أيضا : يجوز أن يكون أهل الكتاب قد اختلفوا في مدة لبثهم كما اختلفوا في عدتهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Another view says the sleepers briefly awoke and then returned to sleep, explaining the increase; al-Ālūsī considers this closer than the solar-versus-lunar reckoning explanation.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنهم انتبهوا قليلا ثم ردوا إلى حالتهم الأولى فلذا ذكر الازدياد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās treats the duration statement as the People of the Book's quoted speculation, not God's assertion; he argues that a true duration would not be followed by saying God knows best, and cites the prior reports as conjecture.
rows.anchor: ونسب ذلك إلى ابن عباس فقد أخرج ابن أبي حاتم وابن مردويه عنه رضي الله تعالى عنه أنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī doubts this attribution: Ibn ʿAbbās accepted the seven-sleepers view even though it too is followed by God's knowing their number, so the same wording cannot distinguish rejection here.
rows.anchor: فقد صح عنه القول بأن عدة أصحاب الكهف سبعة وثامنهم كلبهم مع أنه تعالى عقب القول بذلك بقوله سبحانه ( قل ربي أعلم بعدتهم )

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd's reading says that people said they remained in the cave, supporting the possibility that the duration is quoted speculation; al-Ālūsī still says the following divine statement does not by itself signal rejection.
rows.anchor: نعم قرأ ابن مسعود ( قالوا لبثوا كهفهم ) وهو يقتضي أن يكون من كلام الخائضين

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: On the quoted-speech interpretation, al-Khafājī assigns the pronoun in “they increased” to the People of the Book: some said three hundred, others added nine; al-Ālūsī rejects this as weak.
rows.anchor: وقال الخفاجي : إن ضمير عليه لأهل الكتاب بخلافه على الأول ويظهر فيه وجه العدول

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the suggestion that the nine is unspecified as to years, months, days, or hours: a following unqualified count takes the unit of the preceding explicit number.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنه تعالى ما قال ( وازدادوا تسعا ) كانت التسع مبهمة لا يدري أنها سنون أم شهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative “nine” is the one object of the verb “increased”; although Abū al-Baqāʾ says “increase” can take two objects, its derived form here takes one, as usage reported by al-Rāghib also supports.
rows.anchor: ونصب ( تسعا ) على أنه مفعول ( ازدادوا ) وهو مما يتعدى إلى واحد

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ and Ibn al-Ḥājib parse “years” in the common reading as an accusative substitute for “three hundred”; al-Zamakhsharī instead calls it an explanatory apposition, which the Sea commentary rejects for Basran grammar.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو البقاء وابن الحاجب : هو منصوب على البدلية من ( ثلثمائة )

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some prefer explanatory apposition because substitution would seem to make the number itself unintended; a report says listeners asked whether the three hundred meant days, months, or years, after which “years” was revealed. Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows either parsing.
rows.anchor: وادعى بعضهم أنه أولى من البدلية لأنها تستلزم أن لا يكون العدد مقصودا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: A parsing of “years” as a numeral specification is criticized because it seems to make the stay nine hundred years: the specification should count one item per hundred, and years are plural; al-Ālūsī replies that plural specification follows the underlying collective usage.
rows.anchor: وقيل : على التمييز وتعقب بأنه يلزم عليه الشذوذ من وجهين

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj also allows “years” to modify “hundred” in the genitive, semantically describing the whole number as in an Antarah verse about forty-two milk-camels; the passage continues its grammatical defense in the next segment.
rows.anchor: وجوز الزجاج كون ( سنين ) مجرورا على أنه نعت ( مائة ) وهو راجع في المعنى إلى جملة العدد

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī explains the poetic construction by taking “milch-camel” collectively, allowing its plural adjective to describe the whole numbered group; a collective plural in singular form can specify a numeral, as in “twenty persons.”
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي : لا يمتنع أن يكون الشاعر اعتبر حلوبة جمعا وجعل سودا وصفا لها

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and several others recite “three hundred years” with “years” genitive by annexation; the same objection about making the duration nine hundred would apply only if it were a numeral specification.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي وطلحة ويحيى والأعمش والحسن وابن أبي ليلى وخلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural genitive is possible though uncommon: the plural ending may function like a replacement for the singular's deleted final consonant, and the Quranic reading itself suffices as Arabic evidence despite the lack of another attested example.
rows.anchor: لكن قالوا : إن الجمع المذكور فيها قد أجرى مجرى العاري عن علامة الجمع

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy reads “three hundred year” with the singular genitive, the usual construction, as does the Ibn Masʿūd codex.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي ( ثلثمائة سنة ) بالإضافة والإفراد كما هو الاستعمال الشائع

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk reads “three hundred years” with the nominative plural, understood as the predicate of an omitted “they are.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الضحاك ( ثلثمائة سنون ) بالتنوين ورفع سنون على أنه خبر مبتدأ محذوف

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Abū ʿAmr, in the narration of al-Luʾluʾī, read “nine” with an open tāʾ, a dialectal form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وأبو عمرو في رواية اللؤلؤي عنه ( تسعا ) بفتح التاء وهو لغة فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's unseen encompasses everything hidden in the heavens and earth; because He knows what is hidden, He necessarily knows all other created things as well.
rows.anchor: أي جميع ما غاب فيهما وخفي من أحوال أهلها فالغيب مصدر بمعنى الغائب والخفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forms “How seeing and hearing!” are exclamations spoken within the commanded recitation, not an expression of divine surprise; creatures may truly marvel at God's attributes and acts, as a hadith illustrates.
rows.anchor: صيغتا تعجب والهاء ضميره تعالى والكلام مندرج تحت القول فليس التعجب منه سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrasing indicates that God's sight and hearing are attributes distinct from knowledge: the subtle and gross, small and great, hidden and open are equally unobstructed.
rows.anchor: أن شأن بصره تعالى وسمعه عز وجل وهما صفتان غير راجعتين إلى صفة العلم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say existing and nonexistent things are alike in relation to divine sight and hearing, based on the debated thesis that nonexistent things have thingness.
rows.anchor: بل من الناس من قال : إن المعدوم والموجود في ذلك سواء وهو مبني على شيئية المعدوم

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh parses the forms as originally “became seeing” and “became hearing,” then recast into imperative-shaped exclamations with an explicit subject marked by an extra preposition; the phrase carries a nominative subject and genitive surface form.
rows.anchor: والأصل أبصر وأسمع والهمزة للصيرورة لا للتعدية أي صار ذا بصر وصار ذا سمع

rows.speaker: الرضي
rows.claim: Al-Raḍī objects that Sībawayh's past-tense analysis is unattested and that becoming an attribute is rare, while the added preposition is usual with objects, not subjects.
rows.anchor: قال الرضي : وضعف ذلك بأن الأمر بمعنى الماضي مما لم يعهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī replies that imperative forms can carry a past-like sense, citing al-Zajjāj's explanation of “enough by him” as “take satisfaction in him”; the performative exclamation is also more natural in an imperative shape.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأن كون الأمر بمعنى الماضي مما لم يعهد غير مسلم ألا ترى أن كفى به بمعنى أكتف به

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers the analysis attributed to al-Akhfash and al-Farrāʾ: the form is an imperative to everyone to describe God as seeing and hearing, a reading that suits exclamation better than Sībawayh's account.
rows.anchor: ومذهب الأخفش وعزاه الرضي إلى الفراء أن أفعل في نحو هذا التركيب أمر لفظا ومعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this analysis the subject is an unspecified addressee, the form is fixed because it has become an idiom of exclamation, and the added preposition marks the object; al-Zajjāj's alternative makes the hamza causative but is strained.
rows.anchor: واعتبر الفاعل ضميرا لمأمور وهو كل أحد لأن المراد أنه لظهور الأمر يؤمر كل أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The analyses differ if the preposition is omitted under necessity: Sībawayh's account requires the governed noun to become nominative, while the imperative analysis requires accusative.
rows.anchor: وثمرة الخلاف بين س وغيره تظهر فيما إذا اضطر إلى حذف الباء فعلى مذهب س يلزم رفع مجروره

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya suggests “see by God's religion and hear by it,” with the pronoun referring to guidance or to God; al-Ālūsī rejects this interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية : يحتمل أن يكون معنى الآية

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: ʿĪsā reads both verbs as past tense; Abū Ḥayyān takes the wording as a report rather than an exclamation, meaning God enabled His servants to see and hear through knowledge of Him.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى ( أبصر به وأسمع ) بصيغة الماضي فيهما وخرج ذلك أبو حيان على أن المراد الإخبار

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another possibility takes both forms as comparatives used circumstantially of God, with the pronoun referring to the unseen; it denotes perfect sight and hearing rather than literal comparison, and al-Ālūsī finds it closer than Abū Ḥayyān's reading.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون ( أبصر ) أفعل تفضيل وكذا ( أسمع ) وهو منصوب على الحالية من ضمير له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They have no guardian besides Him” refers generally to the inhabitants of the heavens and earth, whose affairs God alone governs.
rows.anchor: ما لهم ( أي لأهل السموات والأرض المدلول عليه بذكرهما

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya offers several possible referents for “they”: the cave youths, the Prophet's hostile contemporaries, believing people of heaven and earth, or those disputing the sleepers' duration; al-Ālūsī calls these readings weak.
rows.anchor: وجوز ابن عطية أن يعود على معاصري رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من الكفار المشاقين له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording “no guardian … and no one shares His judgment” more forcefully denies a partner than a simpler statement that there is no partner.
rows.anchor: أن ما في النظم الكريم أبلغ في نفي الشريك من أن يقال من ولي ولا شريك

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid reads the verb with yāʾ and jussive ending; Yaʿqūb says he knows no basis, while others explain the form as a pause-like sukūn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد ( ولا يشرك ) بالياء

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Qatāda, and others read with tāʾ and a jussive, as a prohibition against shirk addressed to everyone; if directed to the Prophet it would indirectly admonish others, like the quoted poetic address.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر والحسن وأبو رجاء وقتادة والجحدري وأبو حيوة وزيد وحميد بن الوزير

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The tāʾ reading could address the Prophet and connect to the earlier command not to make a definite promise, meaning to ask no one about the cave story or its duration and rely on revelation; al-Ālūsī finds this far from the apparent construction.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون الخطاب له صلى الله عليه وسلم ويجعل معطوفا على ( لا تقولن )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the cave story was unseen to the Prophet and its inclusion signals revelation and miraculousness, God commands him to keep reciting the Quran to his companions or generally and ignore demands to replace it.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر قصة أصحاب الكهف وكانت من المغيبات بالإضافة إليه صلى الله عليه وسلم ودل اشتمال القرآن عليها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The verb may instead come from “following”: obey and adhere to what was revealed.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون ( أتل ) أمرا من التلو بمعنى الاتباع أي اتبع ما أوحي إليك

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another connection is to the earlier prohibitions on disputing deeply and consulting the People of the Book: recite what revelation says about them, be satisfied with it, and do not prolong argument; this reading means the cave-story verses.
rows.anchor: وقيل وجه الربط أنه سبحانه لما نهاه عن المراء المتعمق فيه وعن الاستفتاء أمره سبحانه بأن يتلو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A weaker proposal attaches the command to “Say, God knows best,” taking the revelation to mean the report of their duration; al-Ālūsī says the intended revelation is broader, including the cave account and the rest of the Book.
rows.anchor: وقيل : متعلق بقوله تعالى : ( قل الله أعلم بما لبثوا ) أي قل لهم ذلك واتل عليهم أخباره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one can alter God's words, though He can erase or confirm what He wills; the statement's broad wording covers reports and commands, understood as the rulings of His words, as al-Ṭabrisī explains.
rows.anchor: لا يقدر أحد علد تبديلها وتغييرها غيره وأما هو سبحانه فقدرته شاملة لكل شيء يمحو ما يشاء ويثبت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not conflict with the Quran's statement that God replaces a verse: reports cannot be abrogated because that would make them false, and al-Rāzī's claim that abrogation is not really alteration is a mistaken evasion.
rows.anchor: والظاهر عموم الكلمات الإخبار وغيرها ومن هنا قال الطبرسي المعنى لا مغير لما أخبر به تعالى ولا لما أمر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some restrict “His words” to God's promises to monotheists, reading the verse as reassurance that God will support the Prophet and his companions against disbelievers; al-Ālūsī finds it contextually apt but unconvincing.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من خص الكلمات بمواعيده تعالى لعباده الموحدين فكأنه قيل اتل ما أوحي إليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “His words” most likely refers to the Book, though it can refer to the Lord; the same Lord is the more apparent referent in the following pronoun.
rows.anchor: والضمير على ما يظهر من مجمع البيان للكتاب ويجوز أن يكون للرب تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You will find no refuge besides Him” means no place to flee to in a calamity; the term derives from leaning or turning aside, and al-Rāghib allows it to be either a place noun or verbal noun.
rows.anchor: أي ملجأ تعدل إليه عند إلمام ملمة وقال الإمام في البيان والإرشاد : وأصله من الالتحاد بمعنى الميل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the refuge as an underground entrance, citing a line by Khuṣayb al-Ḍamrī; al-Ālūsī says there is no need to imagine an earthen tunnel as a hiding place.
rows.anchor: وفسره ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما هنا بالمدخل في الأرض وأنشد عليه حين سأله نافع بن الأزرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the address is to the highest of messengers, the warning is hypothetical: neither he nor his pure companions could find refuge from God; the passage ends as a prayer for divine protection.
rows.anchor: فالكلام مبني على الفرض والتقدير إذ هو عليه الصلاة والسلام بل خلص أمته لا تحدثهم أنفسهم بطلب ملجأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the esoteric reading, the station of servitude is unmatched, and the Prophet reaches its highest rank as the true servant, free of both worlds.
rows.anchor: قد تقدم أن مقام العبودية لا يشابهه مقام ولا يدانيه ونبينا صلى الله عليه وسلم في أعلى مراقيه

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Some esoteric interpreters take “no crookedness” to refer to the Prophet: God made him steadfast in servitude with no turning toward anything besides Him; steadfastness is then a creative divine command.
rows.anchor: وجعله بعض أهل التأويل عائدا على ( عبده ) أي لم يجعل له عليه الصلاة والسلام انحرافا عن جنابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this allegory the severe punishment is the pain of being veiled and distanced from God, the gravest torment, as a verse about people being screened from their Lord also suggests.
rows.anchor: وهو بأس الحجاب والبعد عن الجناب وذلك أشد العذاب ( كلا إنهم عن ربهم يومئذ لمحجوبون )

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The righteous deeds promised reward are actions intended solely for God's sake; an alternative defines them as disowning one's own existence in favor of the Real.
rows.anchor: وهي الأعمال التي أريد بها وجه الله تعالى لا غير وقيل العمل الصالح التبري من الوجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The good reward signifies seeing the Lord and witnessing the Real without a veil.
rows.anchor: وهي رؤية المولى ومشاهدة الحق بلا حجاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's grief when people reject the revelation signals his intense compassion and desire that opponents join the believers.
rows.anchor: فيه إشارة إلى مزيد شفقته صلى الله عليه وسلم واهتمامه وحرصه على موافقة المخالفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rivers, trees, minerals, and animals on earth are its adornment for its inhabitants; the test of best action turns that adornment into a mirror for contemplating divine majesty and beauty.
rows.anchor: من الأنهار الأشجار والمعادن والحيوانات ( زينة لها ( أي لأهلها ( لنبلوهم أيهم أحسن عملا

rows.speaker: ابن عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ defines good action as turning away from everything else.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطاء : حسن العمل الاعتراض عن الكل

rows.speaker: الجنيد
rows.claim: Al-Junayd says good action is to take up worldly adornment without becoming occupied by it.
rows.anchor: وقال الجنيد : حسن العمل اتخاذ ذلك وعدم الاشتغال به

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say God's knowers and lovers adorn the earth, and good action is to regard them with reverence.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : أهل المعرفة بالله تعالى والمحبة له هم زينة الأرض وحسن العمل النظر إليهم بالحرمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The barren plain signifies the world's annihilation becoming manifest when true divine existence and the greater Resurrection appear.
rows.anchor: كناية عن ظهور فناء ذلك بظهور الوجود الحقاني والقيامة الكبرى

rows.speaker: الجنيد
rows.claim: Al-Junayd says the Prophet's night journey and ascension were more wondrous than the cave youths' story: he was taken from Mecca to Jerusalem, reached the Lote Tree and the distance of two bows, then returned before the night ended.
rows.anchor: قال الجنيد قدس الله سره : أي لا تتعجب منهم فشأنك أعجب من شأنهم حيث أسري بك ليلا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The youths are spiritually the young people of gnosis, whose chivalry is to abandon all besides God and retreat into solitude with Him.
rows.anchor: قيل هم فتيان المعرفة الذين جبلوا على سجية الفتوى وفتوتهم إعرتضهم عن غير الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their taste of communion spurs them to seek further ascent through the stations of spiritual bliss.
rows.anchor: هيجهم ما ذاقوا إلى طلب الزيادة والترقي في مراقي السعادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being made to sleep is allegorized as absorption in God and annihilation in everything besides Him.
rows.anchor: كناية عن جعلهم مستغرقين فيه سبحانه فانين به تعالى عما سواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two groups' dispute over the duration signifies return from spiritual intoxication to sobriety, subsistence after annihilation, or disclosure after retreat; the latter pair are close interpretations.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى ردهم إلى الصحو بعد السكر والبقاء بعد الفناء ويقال أيضا : هو إشارة إلى الجلوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their belief is intellectual faith; the increase in guidance means God made them present with Him and unveiled realities to them.
rows.anchor: ( الإيمان العلمي ( وزدناهم هدى ( بأن أحضرناهم وكاشفناهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God steadied their hearts with certainty, removing intrusive guesses and Satanic whispers; another reading says He raised them from spiritual fluctuation to firmness.
rows.anchor: سكناها عن التزلزل بما أسكنا فيها من اليقين فلم يسمح فيها هواجس التخمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their standing is allegorized as standing through God; He alone sustains and governs the heavens and earth, which exist through His generosity.
rows.anchor: إذ قاموا ) بنا لنا ( فقالوا ربنا رب السموات والأرض

rows.speaker: بعض المشايخ
rows.claim: Some shaykhs cite the youths' standing as proof that spiritual seekers should stand while remembering God; Ibn al-Ghars calls the proof weak. Al-Ālūsī allows standing remembrance but condemns the contemporary ritual circles as lacking prophetic precedent and as snares of Satan.
rows.anchor: واستدل بعض المشايخ بهذه الآية على أنه ينبغي للسالكين إذا أرادوا الذكر وتلحقوا له أن يقوموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leaving the people and their worship symbolizes leaving the company of passion and turning away from everything besides God; taking refuge in the cave means retreating into solitude with the Beloved.
rows.anchor: وإذ اعتزلتموهم وما يعبدون إلا الله ) أي وإذ خرجتم عن صحبة أهل الهوى

rows.speaker: بعض العارفين
rows.claim: A gnostic says solitude from everything besides God brings union with Him, which comes only after withdrawal; he compares this to the Prophet's retreat in Ḥirāʾ before revelation.
rows.anchor: قال بعض العارفين : العزلة عن غير الله تعالى توجب الوصلة بالله عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun's turning away preserves spiritual presence by keeping too much light out of the cave; darkness aids contemplation and concentration, so retreatants choose dim places and close their eyes during vigilance.
rows.anchor: لئلا يكثر الضوء في الكهف فيقل معه الحضور فقد ذكروا أن الظلمة تعين على الفكر

rows.speaker: أسرار القرآن
rows.claim: An esoteric reading makes the sun God's majesty, the cave their nearness to Him, and the right and left sides pre-eternity and eternity; the youths are protected from the overwhelming radiance of the divine essence.
rows.anchor: وفي أسرار القرآن أن في الآية إشارة إلى أن الله تعالى حفظهم عن الاحتراق في السبحات

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another reading makes the sun the spirit, gnosis, or sainthood: in ecstatic intoxication the mystics turn from worldly future, and in sobriety they turn from worldly life, avoiding both sides for God.
rows.anchor: وقيل : في تأويله إن شمس الروح أو المعرفة والولاية إذا طلعت من أفق الهداية

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the light of their sainthood repelled sunlight just as a believer's light overcomes Hellfire; though reported from Ibn ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ālūsī calls this baseless.
rows.anchor: وذكر أن فيه إشارة إلى أن نور ولايتهم يغلب نور الشمس ويرده عن الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guided person has had veils lifted and attained success; God leaves the misled without a guiding protector because their deficient readiness makes guidance impossible.
rows.anchor: ( من يهد الله فهو المهتد ( الذي رفعت عنه الحجب ففاز بما فاز

rows.speaker: ابن عطاء
rows.claim: Their apparent wakefulness and sleep signify that their bodies remain among people while their spirits abide with God; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ describes them as beyond time and place, alive and dead, asleep yet alert in the divine presence.
rows.anchor: ( وتحسبهم أيقاظا وهم رقود ( إشارة إلى أنهم مع الخلق بأبدانهم ومع الحق بأرواحهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Turning them right and left can mean moving them between worlds; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says contraction and expansion or gathering and separation, another says annihilation and subsistence or unveiling and concealment, and another compares their surrender to a corpse in a washer's hands.
rows.anchor: ( ونقلبهم ذات اليمين وذات الشمال ( أي ننقلهم من عالم إلى عالم

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
rows.claim: Abū Bakr al-Warrāq says companionship and proximity to the righteous are a great gain even across different species, as shown by God's mention of the dog alongside the cave companions.
rows.anchor: وكلبهم باسط ذراعيه بالوصيد ) قال أبو بكر الوراق : مجالسة الصالحين ومجاورتهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The cave dog can symbolize their souls, asleep and inactive in works, or souls so disciplined that circumstances obey and protect them from harm.
rows.anchor: وقيل أشير بالآية إلى أن كلب نفوسهم نائمة معطلة عن الأعمال

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: A vision of their awe-inspiring divine robe would make an observer flee in terror, like Moses fleeing his transformed staff; the flight is really from God's majesty displayed in that mirror. This is reported from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq.
rows.anchor: وهذا الفرار حقيقة منا لأنه من عظمتنا الظاهرة في هاتيك المرآة كذا قرره غير واحد وروي عن جعفر الصادق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their awakening means a return to sobriety after spiritual intoxication.
rows.anchor: ( وكذلك بعثناهم ) رددناهم إلى الصحو بعد السكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their guess that they had slept a day or part of one reflects absorption that erased awareness of days and the distinction between moon and sun.
rows.anchor: لأنهم كانوا مستغرقين لا يعرفون اليوم من الأمس ولا يميزون القمر من الشمس

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The brief estimate also symbolizes lovers' tendency to count union as short: even a long meeting seems brief, and the cited poem says a life passed without counting nights.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنهم استقلوا أيام الوصال وهكذا شأن عشاق الجمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Returning from intoxication to sobriety and spirituality to embodied life, they seek human food and apply spiritual principles to practical conduct.
rows.anchor: ثم إنهم لما رجعوا من السكر إلى الصحو ومن الروحانية إلى البشرية طلبوا ما يعيش به الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shared purse teaches aspirants not to beg, rebuking mendicant shaykhs who make a habit of asking, perhaps for unlawful money.
rows.anchor: الإشارة فيه أولا إلى أن اللائق بطالبي الله تعالى ترك السؤال ويرد به على المتشيخين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling it “your silver” teaches companions to share resources rather than reserve something for one member, even though one of the youths may have been a shepherd without money.
rows.anchor: وثانيا إلى أن اللائق بهم أن لا يختص أحدهم بشيء دون صاحبه ألا ترى كيف قال قائلهم ( بورقكم هذه )

rows.speaker: ذو النون
rows.claim: Seeking the purest food teaches scrupulousness; Dhū al-Nūn says a knower does not extinguish the light of gnosis with the light of scruple.
rows.anchor: وثالثا إلى أن اللائق بهم استعمال الورع ألا ترى كيف طلب القائل الأزكى وهو على ما في بعض الروايات الأحل ولذلك قال ذو النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī criticizes a shaykh who accepted money certainly taken from an oppressor, claiming the money was like hot coals that cooled hungry seekers, despite the shrine and votive offerings later attached to him.
rows.anchor: والعجب أن رجلا من المتشيخين كان يأخذ من بعض الظلمة دنانير مقطوعا بحرمتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gentle dealing with the food seller teaches good manners and kindness.
rows.anchor: ورابعا إلى أنه ينبغي لهم التواصي بحسن الخلق وجميل الرفق

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Some exegetes say the command means to select delicate food because they had not eaten and coarse food might harm their bodies; others say their spirits from the sacred realm suit only delicate things.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أهل التأويل : إنه أمر باختيار اللطيف من الطعام لأنهم لم يأكلوا مدة

rows.speaker: يوسف بن الحسين
rows.claim: Yūsuf ibn al-Ḥusayn says to buy delicate food for gnostics, while ascetics may eat whatever is found because they are still disciplining themselves; another view contrasts coarse diets of strivers with the gnostic's preference for delicacy.
rows.anchor: وعن يوسف بن الحسين أنه كان يقول : إذا اشتريت لأهل المعرفة شيئا من الطعام فليكن لطيفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says making delicate food a rule impairs spiritual perfection; even if the report about ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Jīlānī is true, it could be accidental or for a lawful reason, and it conflicts with reports of the Prophet and major Companions' simple diet and clothing.
rows.anchor: وعندي أن التزام ذلك يخل بالكمال وما يروى عن الشيخ قدس سره وأمثاله إن صح يحتمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Keeping the matter secret means concealing spiritual realities from people veiled from their light and insight.
rows.anchor: أي من الأغبار المحجوبين عن مطالعة الأنوار والوقوف على الأسرار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being stoned signifies denial, while forced return to the former religion would be a false faith; such a relapse into disbelief would resemble Iblīs's satanic rejection and preclude success.
rows.anchor: إنهم إن يظهروا عليكم يرجموكم ) بأحجار الإنكار ( أو يعيدوكم في ملتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command not to promise an act for tomorrow signifies complete detachment and reliance on God.
rows.anchor: إرشاد إلى محض التجريد والتفريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story says a Sufi master called his disciple foolish for saying “if God wills” after an instruction, asking who the disciple was if God willed it; al-Ālūsī says the verse utterly rejects this, and the view also conflicts with monistic doctrine.
rows.anchor: ويحكى عن بعض كبار الصوفية أنه أمر بعض تلامذته بفعل شيء فقال : أفعله إن شاء الله تعالى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another says the verse bars the Prophet from speaking about ultimate realities without divine permission, advising shaykhs not to speak such truths without recognized signs of authorization.
rows.anchor: وقيل الآية تنهى عن أن يخبر صلى الله عليه وسلم عن الحق دون إذن الحق سبحانه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An esoteric interpretation says to remember God after forgetting the whole universe, including oneself, because remembrance becomes pure only then.
rows.anchor: قيل أي إذا نسيت الكون بأسره حتى نفسك فإن الذكر لا يصفو إلا حينئذ

rows.speaker: الجنيد
rows.claim: Al-Junayd reads the command as remembering after forgetting remembrance itself; true remembrance is annihilation in the Remembered apart from the act of remembering.
rows.anchor: وقيل إذا نسيت الذكر ومن هنا قال الجنيد قدس سره : حقيقة الذكر الفناء بالمذكور عن الذكر

rows.speaker: الجنيد
rows.claim: Al-Junayd says a station above remembrance is nearer to guidance: God describes and remembers the servant before the servant remembers Him.
rows.anchor: وقال قدس سره في قوله تعالى ( وقل عسى أن يهديني ربي لأقرب من هذا رشدا ( إن فوق الذكر منزلة

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Some allegorize the three hundred and nine years as twenty-five years by treating a Quranic year as a month; al-Ālūsī rejects this as baseless, contrary to Muslim consensus and weak in faith, insisting the possible outward duration should stand.
rows.anchor: زعم بعض أهل التأويل أن مجموع ذلك خمس وعشرون سنة واعتبر السنة التي في الآية شهرا

rows.speaker: ابن سينا
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī supports the possibility of the long sleep by citing Ibn Sīnā's report that Aristotle described mystics who experienced a state resembling the cave sleepers before their time.
rows.anchor: ومما يدل على إمكان هذا اللبث أن أبا علي بن سينا ذكر في الباب الزمان من الشفاء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An allegory says direct divine training without shaykhs may take many years, while guidance through them may be completed in forty days or even a few days; al-Ālūsī answers that God can guide without intermediaries in a few hours.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية على ما قيل إشارة إلى أن المزيد الذي يربيه الله سبحانه بلا واسطة المشايخ يصل في مدة مديدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hidden of the heavens and earth means the upper and lower worlds; hiddenness is only relative to creatures, since nothing is unseen to God.
rows.anchor: له ) تعالى شأنه ( غيب السموات ) عالم العلو ( والأرض ) عالم السفل ولا يخفى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say God does not know the unseen because nothing is unseen to Him; al-Ālūsī says such wording must not be used, even with that intended interpretation, because it appears to contradict Quranic verses.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا قال بعضهم : إنه سبحانه لا يعلم الغيب بمعنى أنه لا غيب بالنسبة إليه تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī condemns people who obscure truth through riddles and thereby mislead others.
rows.anchor: وإلى الله تعالى نشكو أقواما ألغزوا الحق وفتنوا بذلك الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exclamation means that God's sight and hearing are incomparable; on a monistic reading His attributes are identical with His essence.
rows.anchor: أي ما أبصره تعالى وما أسمعه لأن صفاته عين ذاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one is a protector besides God because no one acts independently of Him, and He shares His judgment with no one because His power is perfect and others are incapable.
rows.anchor: وما لهم من دونه من ولي ( إد لا فعل لأحد سواه تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Restrain yourself” means hold someone in place, as in the prohibition against confining an animal for target practice; applying it to steadfast endurance is an extended use, not the literal sense, because the verb's transitivity differs.
rows.anchor: أي احبسها وثبتها يقال صبرت زيدا أي حبسته وفي الحديث النهي عن صبر الحيوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being with the people means keeping their company; calling upon God morning and evening is a common way to express constant worship, like saying someone struck morning and evening to mean the whole body.
rows.anchor: ( أي مصاحبة مع الذين ( يدعون ربهم بالغداة والعشي ( أي يعبدونه دائما

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some keep morning and evening literal rather than treating them as all times; these times are singled out because people are distracted by work and are prone to heedlessness.
rows.anchor: وأبقى غير واحد الغداة والعشي على ظاهر هما ولم يرد عموم الأوقات

rows.speaker: إبراهيم
rows.claim: The worship in question is remembrance of God, reported from Ibrāhīm through Mughīra.
rows.anchor: قيل ذكر الله تعالى وروي ذلك من طريق مغيرة عن إبراهيم

rows.speaker: عبيد الله بن عبد الله بن عدي بن الخيار
rows.claim: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAdī ibn al-Khiyār is reported to say the worship is recitation of the Quran.
rows.anchor: وقيل : قراءة القرآن وروي ذلك عن عبيد الله بن عبد الله بن عدي بن الخيار

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr says it means discussing lawful and unlawful matters.
rows.anchor: وأخرج الحكيم الترمذي عن ابن جبير أن المراد بها المفاوضة والحلال والحرام

rows.speaker: ابن عمر ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar and Mujāhid identify the worship as attending the five daily prayers.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عمر ومجاهد هي شهود الصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda specifies the dawn and afternoon prayers; al-Ālūsī says the preceding discussion supports the apparent, literal times.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة شهود صلاة الصبح والعصر وفيما تقدم ما يؤيد ظاهره أولها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people meant are poor Companions, including ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb, Salmān, Ibn Masʿūd, and Bilāl.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالموصول فقراء الصحابة عمار وصهيب وسلمان وابن مسعود وبلال وأضرابهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reported occasion is that Quraysh chiefs, including Umayya ibn Khalaf, offered to listen if the Prophet moved poor believers away because their wool garments smelled.
rows.anchor: قال كفار قريش كأمية بن خلف وغيره من صناديد أهل مكة لو أبعدت هؤلاء عن نفسك لجالسناك

rows.speaker: سلمان
rows.claim: A report from Salmān says the influential converts ʿUyayna ibn Badr and al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis asked the Prophet to sit at the head of the assembly and send away Salmān, Abū Dharr, and the poor Muslims in wool garments so they could listen and learn.
rows.anchor: عن سلمان قال : جاءت المؤلفة قلوبهم إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عيينة بن بدر والأقرع بن حابس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports disagree about the verse's setting: the Quraysh account makes it Meccan, while the Salmān report makes it Medinan; Abū Ḥayyān prefers Meccan because the surah is Meccan, but al-Ālūsī says most reports support Medina and such verses can be exceptions.
rows.anchor: والآية على هذا مدنية وعلى الأول مكية قال أبو حيان : وهو أصح لأن السورة مكية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report through Juwaybir from al-Ḍaḥḥāk attributes the Meccan occasion to Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Ālūsī says the verses that follow may favor the Medinan setting.
rows.anchor: وقد أخرج ما يؤيد الأول ابن مردويه من طريق جويبر عن الضحاك عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative description “those who call their Lord” explains the order to remain with them: their defining devotion warrants continued companionship.
rows.anchor: والتعبير عن أولئك بالموصول لتعليل الأمر بما في حيز الصلة من الخصلة الداعية إلى إدامة الصحبة

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads “in the morning” with the definite article. Sībawayh and al-Khalīl explain this through Arabs' use of the word as an indefinite noun; al-Raḍī says it can be indefinite by agreement, although it is usually a declinable-proper genus name.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر ( بالغدوة ( وخرج ذلك على ما ذكره سيبويه والخليل

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: Some verifiers prefer the first grammatical explanation because making a genus name indefinite is less clear than making a personal proper name indefinite; al-Fannārī objects to treating the month name Rajab this way, and al-Ālūsī leaves the discussion to its proper place.
rows.anchor: واختار بعض المحققين التخريج الأول وقال : إنه أحسن دراية ورواية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse is more emphatic than the parallel command not to drive away those who call upon God morning and evening.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية كما في البحر أبلغ من التي في الأنعام وهي قوله تعالى : ( ولا تطرد الذين يدعون ربهم بالغداة والعشي )

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: “Seeking God's face” means seeking His pleasure and approved obedience, not display or fame; al-Suhaylī explains the metaphor through the turning toward someone one favors and turning away from someone one resents.
rows.anchor: بناء على ما قاله الإمام السهيلي من أن الوجه إذا أضيف إليه تعالى يراد به الرضا والطاعة المرضية مجاز

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Alternative readings take “face” as God's essence with an omitted genitive, or as turning toward Him and seeking nearness; al-Ālūsī prefers the first, pleasure-based interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد بالوجه الذات والكلام على حذف مضاف وقيل : هو بمعنى التوجه
